messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 29
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: In a relationship
- Occupation: Coast Guard
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 69

# The Weight of What He Carries

Marcus is twenty-nine years old and has spent the last six years working as a Coast Guard officer. He is the kind of man who runs toward emergencies — who pulls people from freezing water without hesitating, who reads weather systems and calculates risk with a calm that his colleagues have come to rely on. He is good at his job. He has always believed that the danger in his life would come from the sea.

It came instead from a Tuesday evening in November, fourteen months ago, on a side street three blocks from his apartment. Marcus had finished a late shift and stopped to pick up groceries. Two men approached him from behind. One pressed something hard into the small of his back. They took his wallet, his phone, and his watch — a watch his father had given him when he joined the Coast Guard. The whole thing lasted perhaps ninety seconds. When it was over, Marcus stood alone under a yellow streetlight, completely uninjured, and could not move his legs for what felt like a very long time.

He told almost no one. He filed a police report, called his girlfriend Sofia from a borrowed phone, and by the following morning had constructed a version of the story in which he was fine. He had faced worse, he reasoned. He had pulled a man from a capsized vessel in four-meter swells. He should not be undone by a mugging.

But something had shifted in him that he could not reason away. Walking home from anywhere after dark became impossible. He began taking long, circuitous routes to avoid the block where it happened, then gradually began avoiding the entire neighborhood, then the city center. His world quietly contracted. He stopped going to the gym he had used for four years. He declined invitations from friends and offered Sofia excuses that grew thinner over time. She knows something is wrong, and her patience and worry sit alongside each other in ways that make him feel guilty and cornered.

At work, Marcus functions — but only just. He is hypervigilant in ways that look, on the surface, like professionalism. He scans every face on the dock, positions himself with his back to walls, flinches at sounds that would not have registered before. His supervisor has noted that he seems distracted. What the supervisor cannot see is that Marcus sometimes loses entire minutes to a kind of internal paralysis, replaying the sensation of that pressure in his back, the voice that told him not to turn around. The replays arrive without warning — during a briefing, during dinner, in the dark space between waking and sleep. He has not slept more than four hours consecutively since November.

He feels a pervasive shame that he cannot quite name. He is a man trained to manage crisis. He wears a uniform that represents rescue. And yet he is afraid to walk to the corner store after sunset. He finds himself thinking that the men who robbed him somehow knew something about him that he had not known himself — that underneath the competence and the uniform, there is something that can be stopped cold by ninety seconds and a hard object in the back.

Sofia has noticed the flinching, the distance, the way he checks the locks on their apartment door three and four times before bed. She has asked him, gently and then less gently, to talk to someone. He agreed, eventually, the way a person agrees to something they do not believe will help. He sits now in a therapist's office and speaks carefully, measuring out the story in small amounts, as though too much at once might be dangerous. He still has not told anyone about the watch. That detail, for reasons he cannot explain, feels like the part he is least able to say out loud.
